1366 IEEE TRANSACTIONS ON SMART GRID, VOL. 16, NO. 2, MARCH 2025
Optimizing Hydrogen Systems and Demand
Response for Enhanced Integration of
RES and EVs in Smart Grids
Abdelfatah Ali , Member, IEEE, Mostafa F. Shaaban , Senior Member, IEEE,
and Karar Mahmoud , Senior Member, IEEE
Abstract—Global interest in maximizing the hosting capacity
(HC) of renewable energy sources (RES) while avoiding high
energy curtailment has lately grown in smart grids (SGs). This
trend has been associated with the empowerment of hydrogen
systems (HS) and demand response (DR). In this regard, this
article proposes a new approach to optimally synergize HS and
DR for elevated integration of intermittent RES in SGs. The
proposed approach is predicated on a coordinated management
scheme for various SG control devices, including: a complete
HS (hydrogen tank, water electrolyzer, and fuel cell), hydrogen
load DR, RES energy curtailment, DSTATCOM functionality
of the RES inverters, storage charging rates, and electrical
DR. Additionally, the ﬂexibility of electric vehicles (EVs) with
G2V/V2G functionalities has been considered to support RES
and HS expansion. The proposed approach is formulated as a
multi-objective optimization model that aims to optimize two
competing objective functions, i.e., total costs and HC capacity
of RESs. The simulation results reveal the superiority of the
proposed approach which resulted in a notable HC increase of
up to 17.24%, accompanied by a signiﬁcant cost reduction. The
proposed approach is also applied to deﬁne the optimal number
of HS to maximize RES capacity.
Index Terms —Demand response, hosting capacity, hydrogen
system, renewable energy, smart grid.

I. I NTRODUCTION
R
ECENTLY , more and more renewable energy sources
(RESs), mainly wind and photovoltaic generation
systems, are promoted to be integrated into smart grids (SGs).
In this context, hydrogen systems (HS) and demand response
can play important roles in developing the capabilities of
SGs. Speciﬁcally, HS, as a clean and versatile energy source
and storage, have a potential feature to address intermit-
tency challenges associated with RES generation [1], [2], [3].
The utilization of surplus electricity to produce hydrogen
through water electrolysis technology has the capability to
increase renewable energy penetration towards sustainable
SGs. By leveraging advanced technologies to seamlessly
integrate hydrogen production, storage, and utilization, a
dynamic solution for balancing supply and demand can be
optimally achieved in SGs. Concurrently, demand response
mechanisms can empower consumers to actively participate
in grid optimization by adjusting their energy consumption.
Therefore, the synergy between HS and demand response not
only enhances grid reliability but also contributes to interna-
tional decarbonization efforts [4], [5], [6]. Most importantly,
the hosting capacity (HC) of RES can be maximized without
curtailing excessive energy in SGs.
In the literature, several research studies have been directed
to develop planning models for RES considering HS from
diverse aspects. In [7], the authors have incorporated the elec-
tric network into the interregional hydrogen supply chains due
to its ability to economically provide energy at long distances.
In [8], a planning algorithm for an electricity-hydrogen uniﬁed
energy system has been introduced considering hydrogen
production and storage abilities. [9], a collaborative plan-
ning model for both electricity and transportation systems
is introduced to achieve the overall emission reduction in
both systems considering hydrogen fuel cell vehicles. The
authors of [10] have utilized particle swarm optimization
for the optimal planning of a combined nuclear-renewable
micro-hybrid energy system considering hydrogen storage.
Reference [11] has introduced an optimal operation and
design approach that considers system reliability with var-
ious renewable energy levels while incorporating emerging
devices e.g. electrolysis cells and hydrogen storage tanks.
In [12], power-to-gas devices and plug-in hybrid electric
and hydrogen-powered vehicles have been utilized to form a
hydrogen-electricity energy-sharing model. In [13], an optimal
operation of hydrogen refueling stations has been proposed
to provide frequency ancillary services to the power grid.
The authors of [14] have addressed the coordinated planning
of high-voltage direct current and power-to-hydrogen supply
chains for renewable energy utilization. The authors of [15]
have proposed a coordination planning model of an integrated
energy system and electric vehicles for reducing carbon
emissions. In [16], an optimal planning model is proposed for
the dual-zero microgrid where the seasonal shift of energy
ﬂow is accomplished by the hydrogen storage system. In [17],
an improved particle swarm optimization has been applied to
solve a planning model that includes different energy genera-
tion players, including hydrogen storage systems, photovoltaic
generation, and wind turbines.
Other research studies have focused on empowering the role
of DR programs for RES planning in modern energy systems.
In [18], an optimal electricity-heat system planning model
has been proposed to enhance the accommodation of wind
energy while considering an integrated DR model. The authors
of [19] have introduced a blockchain-based DR management
that provides optimal energy trading between electric vehicles
(EVs) and charging stations. In [20], a day-ahead energy
management model has been proposed for microgrids with a
DR aggregator as an intermediate coordinator to optimize the
social welfare of microgrids while considering the privacy of
end-users. The authors of [21] have formulated a stochastic-
risk model for microgrid participation in various services
markets considering DR while modeling uncertainties of solar
radiation and wind speed. In [22], a novel mixed-integer linear
programming model has been formulated for integrated gen-
eration, storage, and DR expansion planning while capturing
ﬂexibility dynamics. A risk-aware V olt/V AR support model
integrated with a reinforcement learning control scheme has
been proposed in [23] for unbalanced distribution systems
while considering DR and voltage reduction strategies. In [24],
a planning model has been proposed to identify the ideal
DR intensity for multi-carrier microgrids, which can save
energy and provide ﬁnancial proﬁts via tuning energy demands
during peak instant. The authors of [25] have proposed a
coordinative planning model of public transport electriﬁca-
tion and RESs where public transport hubs are modeled as
ﬂexible nodes with DR features. The authors of [26] have
integrated DR with a holistic energy management system with
PV generation and energy storage considering commercial
customers.
The integration of HS, DR, and EVs to maximize the
HC of RES faces several key challenges [27], [28], [29].
Coordinating diverse components like hydrogen tanks (HT),
water electrolyzers (WE), fuel cells (FC), and EVs with grid
interaction features demands advanced control and communi-
cation systems [27]. Scaling such systems for larger grids with
diverse demands presents further challenges. High upfront
costs, regulatory complexities, and maintaining grid stability
amidst renewable energy variability add to the difﬁculty [30].
Managing data, gaining public acceptance, and building tech-
nical expertise also pose signiﬁcant challenges [31]. Therefore,
to effectively address these challenges, several key approaches
can be utilized. Adopting a holistic energy system plan-
ning approach that considers different assets enables the
efﬁcient utilization and advancement of RES within the
smart grid [32]. Also, conducting comprehensive techno-
economic analysis across the entire hydrogen supply chain
allows for informed decision-making by evaluating economic,
environmental, and societal factors, thus maximizing overall
beneﬁts while minimizing risks [33]. Moreover, implementing
energy management systems tailored to industrial clusters
minimizes operational costs and maximizes green hydrogen
production, enhancing the economic viability of sustainable
energy solutions [34]. These strategies collectively contribute
to the transition towards a greener and more efﬁcient energy
landscape while addressing key challenges in integrating
complex systems into diverse grids.

TABLE I
MAJOR FEATURES OF PROPOSED AND PREVIOUSLY
PLANNING APPROACHES
As mentioned above, extensive studies and different plan-
ning models have been directed to maximize the RES HC
in the modern grid. However, most of these approaches
focus on empowering either the HS or DR. It is worth
mentioning that the simultaneous consideration of both HS
and DR can provide further technical and economic beneﬁts
to the SGs, but requires precise modeling of a such complex
problem with a low computational burden. A complete HS
modeling is required that includes the hydrogen tank, water
electrolyzer, and fuel cell to represent the real-time interactions
with the grid. Other approaches adopt unrealistic assumptions
for mitigating complexity, i.e., utilizing deterministic RES
and load models, ignoring the reactive power support by
RES inverters, and RES energy curtailment. In addition,
many of the existing studies fail to incorporate the ﬂexibility
of EV charging stations in the planning model, yielding
reduced beneﬁts. In turn, these extra beneﬁts must come
with a more detailed modeling of the stochastic nature of
EVs while empowering the controlled charging/discharging
features. Most importantly, it is required to model the tradeoff
between two competing objective functions: total costs (HS
cost, RES cost, charging/discharging cost of EVs, DR discom-
fort cost, and curtailment costs of hydrogen and RESs) and
HC of energy source in SGs.
To cover the research gap in the literature review, in this
paper, the authors suggest a planning model to combine
HS and DR in the best possible way to maximize the
integration of intermittent photovoltaic and wind power in
SGs. To accomplish this goal, a coordinated management
scheme for multiple SG control devices is incorporated into
the proposed planning model, which is missing in most
existing approaches. To highlight the contribution of the paper,
the major features of the proposed planning approach are
compared with the previously planning approaches in Table I.
The adopted control devices include 1) storage charging rates,
2) electrical DR (EDR), 3) hydrogen load DR (HDR), 4) RES
energy curtailment options, and 5) DSTATCOM functionality
of the RES interfacing inverters. Besides, a set of the control
variables of a complete HS (including the HT, WE, and FC)
are formulated in the planning model for SGs. Furthermore,
precise modeling that allows for further RES and HS growth in
SGs has been taken into consideration for the charging stations
of EVs with G2V/V2G features. The suggested approach is

designed to maximize two conﬂicting objective functions—
the overall costs and the HC of RESs using a multi-objective
optimization framework. A mixed probability model that takes
into account a realistic yearly dataset has been developed to
reﬂect different uncertainties and give accurate locations and
capacity for both hydrogen and renewable energy systems.
Several simulation examples and comparisons with other
models show the effectiveness of the suggested planning
model. The results of the simulations demonstrate how well
the suggested approach performs in providing high renewable
energy penetration with appropriate HS at the lowest possible
cost. An important extension for the proposed model has been
highlighted, which is accurately deﬁning the best number of
HS in a certain SG to maximize RES size.
II. P
ROBLEM DESCRIPTION
SGs are being formed based on an active network con-
cept where various forms of energy sources and storage are
integrated efﬁciently besides load centers. For instance, Fig. 1
depicts a visual representation of an SG in which PV and wind
systems are considered energy sources supplying different load
types (including ﬂexible loads) while EV charging stations
and HS are ﬂexible energy storage systems. Such ﬂexibility
of distributed generation (Watt-V Ar control functions), storage
(charging/discharging ﬂexibility), and load (DR options) can
have signiﬁcant positive impacts in improving SG performance
with optimized operational costs. For this purpose, an SG
management unit is considered which controls the energy ﬂow
and is responsible for energy generation, distribution, storage,
and trading. In this work, we aim to empower such emerging
SG ﬂexibility to optimally plan RES units (PV and wind
turbines) as well as HS in a simultaneous manner for efﬁcient
and economic operation.
III. P
ROPOSED APPROACH
In this section, the mathematical formulation of the
proposed multi-objective optimization model is presented.
Maximizing the HC of RES is essential for a sustainable,
low-carbon future, improving energy security, and driving eco-
nomic growth. Additionally, it represents a pivotal step towards
achieving climate goals, fostering cleaner environments, and
advancing innovation in energy technologies. The proposed
model aims to optimize the planning of RES and HS to

C. Modeling Uncertainty in RES and Load Demand
This subsection models the uncertainties associated with
RES load demand. We have considered a study period of one
year, which is divided into four seasons, with a representative
day generated for each season to capture the random behavior
of various RES and load demand during each season. The
Beta probability distribution function (PDF) is applied to
represent solar irradiance variability, while the Rayleigh PDF
characterizes the stochasticity of wind speed. Conversely,
the normal PDF is used to capture the uncertainty in load
demand [36], [37], [38]. The study leverages hourly historical
data spanning three years encompassing solar irradiance,
wind speed, and load demand. Each year is split into four
seasons, with each season being represented by any day within
that season. The data are then used to create a frequency
distribution of the irradiance, wind speed, and load demand
measurements for each season’s typical day. Each day is
divided into 24 hourly segments, resulting in a total of 96-
time segments for the year (24 hours per season). Assuming
each month has 30 days, each time segment contains 270
(3 months× 30 days/month × 3 years) solar irradiance, wind
speed, and load demand data points. The mean and standard
deviation for each time segment are calculated utilizing these
data. Then, the Beta, Weibull, and normal PDFs are generated
for each hour.
It is worth mentioning that the impact of changing
environmental conditions and grid dynamics can introduce
uncertainties. However, considering such changing environ-
mental conditions and grid dynamics, it can signiﬁcantly
increase the computational burden of the proposed planning
approach. Accordingly, this assumption (historical data for
probability modeling) is followed for the sake of applicability,
where it is widely adopted in the literature [37], [39], [40].
